argument:
Aristotle came to Athens at seventeen, after his father died, and stayed twenty years in Plato's Academy. He inherited his teacher's central question: how can we recognize a tree as a tree when no two trees are alike? Plato's answer was the world of forms, a realm of perfect originals reachable only by reason. When Plato died and the Academy passed him over for Plato's nephew, who held more orthodox views, Aristotle left. Stephen West treats the departure as the best thing that ever happened to him, since it let him follow his own instincts at last. He tutored the thirteen-year-old Alexander of Macedon, later founded the Lyceum, and eventually was exiled from Athens for Macedonian sympathies. The host also takes on the ugly parts directly: Aristotle's defenses of slavery and of women's inferiority rested on bad biology, including the belief that semen supplied a baby's form and the mother only the matter.

The clearest picture of the split is Raphael's The School of Athens, where Plato points at the sky and Aristotle holds a hand flat above the ground. Plato was a rationalist and a mathematician, at home with perfect circles no eye has ever seen. Aristotle was an empiricist and a biologist, and biology is done by looking. So tree-y-ness, for him, is not a copy of something in heaven. It is the set of similarities running through every tree you have ever seen, assembled by your senses over a lifetime. The same goes for virtue. No baby is born knowing temperance. A kid learns it when his parents pry him off Angry Birds, or when his father says he only eats one cookie a day because things are good in moderation.

That commitment shapes Aristotle's account of existence. Greenness and smoothness do not float free; they exist only in some physical thing that is green or smooth. And asking what a thing is made of, the obsession of Thales and Democritus, gets you only a quarter of the way. Aristotle's four causes cover a bridge completely: the material is concrete and steel, the formal is the architect's design, the efficient is the construction crew, the final is getting people across the chasm. The final cause is teleology, and Aristotle refused to skip even a mealworm, quoting Heraclitus telling nervous visitors that there were gods even in his kitchen. Purpose is also what makes evaluation possible. A good ear is one that hears well.

Sorting animals meant repeating the same deductions until Aristotle noticed the pattern and wrote down the first formal system of logic, the Organon, whose title means "the instrument." He preferred variables to examples; the famous "Socrates is mortal" syllogism actually comes from Sextus Empiricus. Pair deduction with induction and you get his scientific method, aimed not at facts but at causes. His taxonomy stood 1,500 years, his logic nearly two millennia. West closes on a walk, a discarded definition, and a question: what is beauty?
keyIdeas: Where Plato believed truth is accessed through reason toward a transcendent world of forms, Aristotle believed truth is found on earth through the senses -- symbolized in Raphael's The School of Athens by Plato pointing up and Aristotle's hand held parallel to the ground.
Aristotle rejected Plato's innate knowledge: our sense of 'tree-y-ness' (or any universal concept) is built up from the sum of our sensory experience, not remembered from a heavenly realm.

Aristotle's four causes explain any existing thing: material cause (what it's made of), formal cause (its arrangement or structure), efficient cause (what brought it into being), and final cause (its purpose or function).

Considering an object's final cause mattered for classification because two creatures with very different appearances could share functionally similar features that place them in the same category, which physical traits alone would miss.

Aristotle's scientific method combined inductive reasoning (using observed patterns to arrive at premises believed true) with deductive reasoning via the syllogism (transforming those premises into proven universal truths).

The study of the purpose or function (final cause) that natural things serve, central to how Aristotle classified living things.
